Question 1 of 11 · Is there a Creator?

Can we know that anything is real?

Short answer

Yes. Even doubting proves that something is real, and no one lives as if nothing is.

Objections

What people say against this, and our answer. Open one to read it.

You might say“Reality itself might not exist”

Our answer

Even your doubt is proof that something is real.

The one thing you cannot doubt

René Descartes tried to doubt everything — his senses, the physical world, even mathematics. But he hit a wall: to doubt, you must be thinking. To be thinking, you must exist. "I think, therefore I am" (Cogito ergo sum) is the one statement that survives total skepticism. The experience of uncertainty is itself undeniably real.

This doesn't mean we have perfect knowledge of reality. It means that something exists — including you, your experience, and the act of questioning. That's enough to build on.

Read more

The philosophical position that nothing can be known is called Pyrrhonian skepticism. Its ancient critics pointed out a fatal flaw: the claim "nothing can be known" is itself a knowledge claim. If it's true, we know it — which contradicts it. Complete skepticism collapses under its own weight.

You might say“I just can't be certain about anything”

Our answer

Total skepticism is a position no one actually lives by.

The gap between theory and practice

The ancient Pyrrhonian skeptics were criticized for leading to apraxia — the inability to act. If you genuinely can't know whether fire burns, you can't decide not to touch it. The philosopher David Hume, one of history's greatest skeptics, acknowledged this himself: after an afternoon of radical philosophy, he would go play backgammon and forget his doubts. Nature, he said, forces us back to common life.

You avoid cars, trust floors to hold you, expect the sun to rise. These aren't leaps of faith — they're rational inferences from consistent experience. The consistency of reality is itself evidence worth examining. A reality that behaves according to stable, mathematical laws points to something deeper than randomness.

Read more

Certainty is not the standard required for rational belief. We don't need absolute proof that the sun will rise tomorrow — overwhelming consistent evidence is sufficient. The same standard applies to the question of whether a Creator exists. We're not looking for mathematical proof; we're weighing evidence. And the evidence — the existence of the universe, its fine-tuning, its rational order — is substantial.

You might say“Maybe we're living in a simulation”

Our answer

If we're in a simulation, that confirms a Creator — it doesn't remove one.

Simulation theory and the question of origins

Philosopher Nick Bostrom's simulation argument (2003) suggests that if advanced civilisations can run simulations of minds, we are probably in one. But notice what this implies: the simulation had to be designed by someone. That designer is real, exists outside our reality, and brought our reality into being. The simulation hypothesis doesn't eliminate God — it describes God.

The simulation hypothesis also pushes the question back rather than answering it. Who created the civilisation that runs the simulation? What are the physical laws of their reality? You still need a first cause — an uncaused originator — at some level. Moving the origin of our universe one level up doesn't escape the need for an ultimate beginning.

Read more

Interestingly, many Muslim thinkers note that the Quran already describes existence as something created, sustained, and perceived through faculties given to us by a Creator — not as independently self-existing. In that sense, Islam has always held that the reality we experience is contingent on a higher reality. Whether that's called "the base reality" or "the simulation's host universe" doesn't change the fundamental question: what caused it?
